claims.text: Trace oxygen or similar impurities segregate at nanoparticle surfaces and interfaces.
Impurity segregation lowers the local energy barrier for premelting and melting in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are solid, impurity-low, and elementally uniform.
Trace impurity content can be varied through synthesis or post-synthesis processing.
Oxygen or other impurity atoms migrate to surfaces and interfaces during heating.
Trace interstitial impurities can promote phase segregation during thermal exposure.
Impurity segregation creates localized regions of weakened atomic bonding at nanoparticle surfaces or grain boundaries.
Impurity-induced phase segregation locally reduces cohesive energy.
The local reduction in cohesive energy triggers early localized liquid-phase formation.
Moderate oxygen exposure causes an earlier premelting onset than in impurity-low FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
Moderate oxygen exposure makes premelting more gradual and produces early liquid-like interfacial regions.
FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles maintained under ultra-high vacuum exhibit a sharper melting transition at a higher temperature.
High-purity, impurity-minimized FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles have a sharp, relatively high, well-defined melting temperature.
The proposed mechanism applies to high-surface-area-to-volume nanoparticles heated near their premelting and melting regimes.
The impurity concentration threshold and nanoscale segregation kinetics have not yet been quantified.
A lack of statistically significant oxygen-induced reduction in premelting onset or change in transition progression would falsify the proposed mechanism.
